title: Adjudicative policymaking and unfair retroactivity
summary: An agency may develop policy in adjudication, but reliance, burdens, and the governing statute can constrain retroactive application or require rulemaking.
notes:
Chenery II allows agencies to develop statutory standards through particular cases when Congress has not mandated a different method. Its rationale includes unforeseen problems, limited prior experience, and factual variation. Bell Aerospace confirms that general implications do not alone require a rule, while preserving statutory and abuse-of-discretion limits.

The assigned Clark-Cowlitz discussion supplies five nonexclusive factors for manifest injustice: whether the issue is one of first impression; whether the rule abruptly departs from established practice or fills an unsettled area; actual reliance on the former rule; the burden of retroactivity; and the statutory interest in applying the new approach. These are a D.C. Circuit formulation, not a claim that every court applies an identical checklist. Fines or damages for conduct undertaken in good-faith reliance especially sharpen the concern.

Congress can expressly require rulemaking or design an enabling statute that has no operative prohibition until regulations exist. The Public Health Service Act example illustrates that statutory authority to make and enforce regulations is not necessarily an immediately enforceable command against private conduct. The agency’s procedural choice therefore begins with the substance and structure of the particular grant.
